effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative comparative case study; no statistical point estimates, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across both an unplanned settlement (Izbet ElHaggana, after formal state pipe installation and meter registration in 2013) and an elite planned suburb (ElTagammo' ElKhames in New Cairo), formalization and privatization failed to deliver reliable water supply, leaving residents facing frequent rationing, week-long or monthly/bimonthly cutoffs, degraded water quality ('yellowed water' in decaying community pipes), and fragmented institutional accountability. Both marginalized and elite residents relied on hybrid informal practices (gehood zateya) to maintain water access and secure repairs: community self-help ashwa'i pipelines, communal hoses, rooftop storage, and informal payments to truck drivers and municipal engineers in ElHaggana, and retired military/police compound liaisons, personal patronage networks (wasta), and developer intermediaries in New Cairo.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 10–16, Section 'Results: Repair and decay in Haganna and Tagammo’'; PDF pp. 16–19, Conclusion and Highlights

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative study appraised with CASP Qualitative Checklist (design ceiling = 2). Through 72 interviews, community visits, and narrative walks, the author directly documents the administrative and institutional mechanisms (formalization without maintenance, fragmented utility/municipal/developer jurisdiction, unresponsive complaint hotlines, discretionary scheduling, bribes, and patronage/wasta networks) shaping water access, reliability, and repair delays.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 8–9, Section 'Research methods and context'; PDF pp. 10–16, Section 'Results: Repair and decay in Haganna and Tagammo’'

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines formalization of unplanned squatted settlements vs master-planned suburbs (tenure, planning), utility/maintenance fees and informal repair bribes (fees), slow municipal/utility repair waits (delay), arbitrary shutoffs and priority repair/water-truck routing via bribes and wasta (discretion), hotline and Facebook complaints deflected between state utilities and private developers (complaint), community self-help networks/funds and owners' associations (participation), splintered governance across GCWC, New Urban Communities Authority, municipality (gehaz), and developers (institutional_fragmentation), compound military/police liaisons and developer-bureaucracy patronage ties (political_coordination), and supply cutoffs alongside household self-disconnection and digging to reconnect to informal ashwa'i pipes (disconnection, reconnection).
